 Superintendent backs keeping current school holidays 
 by Zane Razzaq November 20, 2026 November 20, 2026 
 Superintendent Bella Wong at a public comment during a Brookline School Committee Meeting in Brookline, MA on Thursday, April 16, 2026. Photo by Andrew Burke-Stevenson 
 Superintendent Bella Wong is recommending the district keep its existing religious and cultural holidays on the school calendar, while most families who responded to a district survey favored a calendar observing only state and federal holidays.
 Wong, who presented her recommendation to the School Committee on Nov. 12 , said her endorsement is shaped by concerns about staff and student attendance, students falling behind for missing school, and the district’s commitment to an inclusive environment.
 “When we think about belonging and being inclusive, sometimes it may mean we inconvenience ourselves to be able to do that,” said Wong.
 The five religious and cultural holidays that would become regular school days under a calendar observing only state and federal holidays are Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Eid al-Fitr, Lunar New Year, and Good Friday.
 Lunar New Year was added for the 2020-21 school year, while Eid al-Fitr was added for the 2025-26 school year.
 The School Committee is considering options for the 2027-28 academic calendar. It must vote by its last meeting before February vacation, according to its official policy manual.
 The decision will come as part of an ongoing discussion about how to balance cultural inclusion with the practical challenges of scheduling the school year. 
 The School Committee voted in 2024 to close schools on Eid al-Fitr, an Islamic holiday which celebrates the end of Ramadan. Last year, an intense debate followed about whether to recognize religious holidays (other than those federally celebrated) at all. 
 What did the survey find?

 According to district survey results, 62% of responding households favored a calendar that observed only state and federal holidays when considering their own household. That percentage dipped to 56% when they were asked to consider the broader community beyond their own household.
 29% of families in the district responded to the survey. 
 Staff were nearly evenly split when considering only their own households: 50.4% supported a calendar observing only state and federal holidays and 49.6% favoring keeping the current calendar. When asked to consider the needs of the district and broader community, 56% of responding staff favored retaining the current calendar, compared with 43.1% who preferred observing only state and federal holidays.
 Wong noted that families who responded to the survey likely feel strongly about the issue and suggested that those who did not participate may have more flexibility.
 “So, we are going to assume that the people who responded this is a very important topic for them,” said Wong.
 Wong also raised concerns that eliminating religious holidays could lead to significant student and staff absences, particularly on Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and Good Friday. She said that high absenteeism could make it hard to operate schools safely and result in teachers postponing important instructional material.
 School Committee and public weigh in 
 School Committee member Carolyn Thall pointed to concerns among families who favor a more streamlined calendar, arguing that the district has added too many days off.
 “That would be the case if it was St. Patrick’s Day or Diwali or the first night of Passover,” she said. “It’s important to listen to the broad perspectives that we’ve heard and the reasons people are talking about this are practical reasons and to imply otherwise is unfortunate.”
 The district provides accommodations for students observing religious holidays when schools remain open, including excused absences and restrictions on scheduling homework, tests, and assignment deadlines around certain holidays.
 Member Faiza Khan said the schools set the tone for the broader community and argued that Brookline should consider its collective values rather than approaching the calendar from an individual household’s perspective.
 She also cautioned against relying too heavily on numerical data to make decisions involving equity.
 “If we do too much analysis, it can lead us to paralysis,” said Khan.
 During public comment, Emily Jaffe, co-chair of the Brookline Special Education Parent Advisory Council, said that a calendar designed to promote inclusion can also create inequities for working families and students with disabilities.
 She said working families, especially single parents, may be forced to take unpaid leave or pay for expensive childcare when schools close. She also noted 18% of the district’s students receive special education services and argued that interruptions can disproportionately affect students who require consistent structure and specialized support.
 Chi Chi Wu, chair of the Brookline Asian American Family Network, challenged the argument that the added holidays were primarily responsible for the fragmented calendar. She pointed out that none of the religious and cultural holidays under debate occur in November, despite repeated complaints about the limited number of full days in that month.
 She also underlined the importance of Lunar New Year to Brookline’s Asian American communities, noting that Asian American students make up nearly a quarter of the district’s enrollment and that students themselves had advocated for the holiday’s recognition.
 “All of a sudden, when the holidays of other communities are added, it’s too much,” she said. “That doesn’t feel right. It doesn’t feel inclusive. It doesn’t feel respectful.”
 Brookline High School junior Maryam Keshk, who previously advocated for Eid al-Fitr to become a school holiday, said eliminating the closure would force Muslim students to choose between observing their faith and keeping up with schoolwork.
 Sarah Barrett, a single parent of a child with significant learning disabilities, said that frequent school closures disrupt the structure and routines her child depends on while also creating financial and logistical burdens for families who cannot easily take time off work or afford child care.
 Wong’s recommended calendar would have staff return to school Aug. 31 next year, with students beginning classes Sept. 2, before Labor Day. The earliest possible last day of school under this option would be June 16, depending on snow days.
 Wong also presented options for starting school after Labor Day and eliminating the five religious and cultural holidays, which could allow the school year to end earlier.
 The calendar also cannot be finalized until the district resolves ongoing discussions with the Brookline Educators Union over the number of early release days, which are governed by the educators’ collective bargaining agreement.
